claim: The Mediator complex has been described as a general transcription factor.
source: The Mediator complex has been described as a general transcription factor, but it is unclear if it is essential for Pol II transcription and/or is a required component of the preinitiation complex (PIC) in vivo.
evidence: This is a statement from the abstract that references existing literature characterizing Mediator.

claim: It is unclear if Mediator is essential for Pol II transcription in vivo.
source: The Mediator complex has been described as a general transcription factor, but it is unclear if it is essential for Pol II transcription and/or is a required component of the preinitiation complex (PIC) in vivo.
evidence: This statement identifies a gap in knowledge that the study addresses.

claim: It is unclear if Mediator is a required component of the preinitiation complex (PIC) in vivo.
source: The Mediator complex has been described as a general transcription factor, but it is unclear if it is essential for Pol II transcription and/or is a required component of the preinitiation complex (PIC) in vivo.
evidence: This statement identifies a gap in knowledge that the study addresses.

claim: Depletion of individual Mediator subunits, even those essential for cell growth, causes a general but only modest decrease in transcription.
source: Here, we show that depletion of individual subunits, even those essential for cell growth, causes a general but only modest decrease in transcription.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Simultaneous depletion of all Mediator modules causes a drastic decrease in transcription.
source: In contrast, simultaneous depletion of all Mediator modules causes a drastic decrease in transcription.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7.

claim: Depletion of head or middle subunits causes a downstream shift in the Pol II occupancy profile.
source: Depletion of head or middle subunits, but not tail subunits, causes a downstream shift in the Pol II occupancy profile, suggesting that Mediator at the core promoter inhibits promoter escape.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Depletion of tail subunits does not cause a downstream shift in the Pol II occupancy profile.
source: Depletion of head or middle subunits, but not tail subunits, causes a downstream shift in the Pol II occupancy profile, suggesting that Mediator at the core promoter inhibits promoter escape.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Mediator at the core promoter inhibits promoter escape.
source: Depletion of head or middle subunits, but not tail subunits, causes a downstream shift in the Pol II occupancy profile, suggesting that Mediator at the core promoter inhibits promoter escape.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the downstream shift in Pol II occupancy upon Mediator depletion.

claim: A functional PIC and Pol II transcription can occur when Mediator is not detected at core promoters.
source: Interestingly, a functional PIC and Pol II transcription can occur when Mediator is not detected at core promoters.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Mediator is essential for Pol II transcription.
source: These results provide strong evidence that Mediator is essential for Pol II transcription and stimulates PIC formation, but it is not a required component of the PIC in vivo.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the triple depletion experiments shown in Figure 7.

claim: Mediator stimulates PIC formation.
source: These results provide strong evidence that Mediator is essential for Pol II transcription and stimulates PIC formation, but it is not a required component of the PIC in vivo.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on experimental data throughout the manuscript.

claim: Mediator is not a required component of the PIC in vivo.
source: These results provide strong evidence that Mediator is essential for Pol II transcription and stimulates PIC formation, but it is not a required component of the PIC in vivo.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experiments showing transcription occurs when Mediator is not detected at promoters (Figure 4).

claim: Mediator is a highly conserved, transcriptional co-activator complex.
source: Mediator is a highly conserved, transcriptional co-activator complex that physically bridges activator proteins bound at enhancers and Pol II bound at the promoter (Allen and Taatjes, 2015; Plaschka et al., 2015; Robinson et al., 2015; Jeronimo et al., 2016; Petrenko et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: Mediator physically bridges activator proteins bound at enhancers and Pol II bound at the promoter.
source: Mediator is a highly conserved, transcriptional co-activator complex that physically bridges activator proteins bound at enhancers and Pol II bound at the promoter (Allen and Taatjes, 2015; Plaschka et al., 2015; Robinson et al., 2015; Jeronimo et al., 2016; Petrenko et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: In yeast, Mediator is recruited efficiently to enhancers by many activator proteins that mediate diverse stress responses.
source: In yeast, Mediator is recruited efficiently to enhancers by many activator proteins that mediate diverse stress responses (Bhoite et al., 2001; Bryant and Ptashne, 2003; Kuras et al., 2003; Fan et al., 2006), but poorly by activators that control ribosomal protein or glycolytic genes under optimal growth conditions (Fan et al., 2006; Grünberg et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: Mediator is recruited poorly by activators that control ribosomal protein or glycolytic genes under optimal growth conditions.
source: In yeast, Mediator is recruited efficiently to enhancers by many activator proteins that mediate diverse stress responses (Bhoite et al., 2001; Bryant and Ptashne, 2003; Kuras et al., 2003; Fan et al., 2006), but poorly by activators that control ribosomal protein or glycolytic genes under optimal growth conditions (Fan et al., 2006; Grünberg et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Mediator directly interacts with Pol II.
source: In addition, Mediator directly interacts with Pol II, and it can stimulate preinitiation complex (PIC) assembly, phosphorylation of the Pol II C-terminal domain (CTD) by TFIIH, and basal transcription in vitro (Thompson et al., 1993; Kim et al., 1994; Guidi et al., 2004; Takagi and Kornberg, 2006; Esnault et al., 2008; Malik et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: Mediator can stimulate preinitiation complex (PIC) assembly in vitro.
source: In addition, Mediator directly interacts with Pol II, and it can stimulate preinitiation complex (PIC) assembly, phosphorylation of the Pol II C-terminal domain (CTD) by TFIIH, and basal transcription in vitro (Thompson et al., 1993; Kim et al., 1994; Guidi et al., 2004; Takagi and Kornberg, 2006; Esnault et al., 2008; Malik et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: Mediator can stimulate phosphorylation of the Pol II C-terminal domain (CTD) by TFIIH in vitro.
source: In addition, Mediator directly interacts with Pol II, and it can stimulate preinitiation complex (PIC) assembly, phosphorylation of the Pol II C-terminal domain (CTD) by TFIIH, and basal transcription in vitro (Thompson et al., 1993; Kim et al., 1994; Guidi et al., 2004; Takagi and Kornberg, 2006; Esnault et al., 2008; Malik et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: Mediator can stimulate basal transcription in vitro.

evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: In yeast cells, the PIC has been defined experimentally as the entity that contains Mediator and general transcription factors bound to the core promoter in vivo.

claim: The PIC is short-lived (estimated as 1/8 s).
source: However, the PIC is short-lived (estimated as 1/8 s by Wong et al., 2014), because Mediator only transiently associates with the core promoter; it rapidly dissociates from the PIC upon TFIIH-mediated phosphorylation of the Pol II CTD (Jeronimo and Robert, 2014; Wong et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Mediator only transiently associates with the core promoter.
source: However, the PIC is short-lived (estimated as 1/8 s by Wong et al., 2014), because Mediator only transiently associates with the core promoter; it rapidly dissociates from the PIC upon TFIIH-mediated phosphorylation of the Pol II CTD (Jeronimo and Robert, 2014; Wong et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Mediator rapidly dissociates from the PIC upon TFIIH-mediated phosphorylation of the Pol II CTD.

evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: TFIIH-dependent dissociation of Mediator is important for efficient escape of Pol II from the promoter into the elongation phase of transcription.

source: Upon Mediator dissociation and promoter escape of Pol II, the other general transcription factors remain at the core promoter as a post-escape complex (Wong et al., 2014).

claim: Mediator consists of 25 subunits in S. cerevisiae.

claim: Mediator subunits are organized in 4 modules: the head, middle, tail and kinase modules.
source: Mediator consists of 25 subunits in S. cerevisiae (Bourbon et al., 2004) that are organized in 4 modules: the head, middle, tail and kinase modules (Allen and Taatjes, 2015; Plaschka et al., 2015; Robinson et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The head module interacts with Pol II.
source: The head module interacts with Pol II, and many head and some middle subunits are essential for yeast cell growth.

claim: Many head and some middle subunits are essential for yeast cell growth.
source: The head module interacts with Pol II, and many head and some middle subunits are essential for yeast cell growth.
evidence: This statement is supported by established knowledge in the field.

claim: The tail module directly contacts transcriptional activators.
source: The tail module directly contacts transcriptional activators, and loss of one or more tail subunits impairs but does not eliminate cell growth, although activator-dependent transcription can be affected (Zhang et al., 2004; Ansari et al., 2012; Paul et al., 2015).

claim: Loss of one or more tail subunits impairs but does not eliminate cell growth.
source: The tail module directly contacts transcriptional activators, and loss of one or more tail subunits impairs but does not eliminate cell growth, although activator-dependent transcription can be affected (Zhang et al., 2004; Ansari et al., 2012; Paul et al., 2015).

claim: The kinase module has modest negative or positive effects on selected genes.
source: The kinase module has modest negative or positive effects on selected genes, and cells lacking this module grow well under many conditions (Nemet et al., 2014).

claim: Cells lacking the kinase module grow well under many conditions.

claim: During transcriptional activation, Mediator undergoes a compositional change in which the kinase module dissociates from the remainder of the complex upon interaction with Pol II.

claim: Dissociation of the kinase module from the remainder of the Mediator complex is not rate-limiting for transcription.
source: During transcriptional activation, Mediator undergoes a compositional change in which the kinase module dissociates from the remainder of the complex upon interaction with Pol II; however, this dissociation is not rate-limiting for transcription (Jeronimo et al., 2016; Petrenko et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Mediator is required for yeast cell growth.
source: Mediator is required for yeast cell growth and is often considered to be a general transcription factor like TBP, TFIIB, and Pol II itself (Thompson and Young, 1995; Takagi and Kornberg, 2006).

claim: Mediator is often considered to be a general transcription factor like TBP, TFIIB, and Pol II itself.
source: Mediator is required for yeast cell growth and is often considered to be a general transcription factor like TBP, TFIIB, and Pol II itself (Thompson and Young, 1995; Takagi and Kornberg, 2006).

claim: The issue of whether Mediator is essential for Pol II transcription in vivo is controversial and unresolved.
source: However, the issue of whether Mediator is essential for Pol II transcription in vivo is controversial and unresolved, largely because it has been addressed almost exclusively with a temperature-sensitive (ts) mutation of the essential subunit Med17(Srb4).
evidence: This statement identifies a gap in knowledge that the study addresses.

claim: Loss of Med17 function at the restrictive temperature reduces mRNA levels to the same extent as observed for a ts mutation of Pol II.
source: Loss of Med17 function at the restrictive temperature reduces mRNA levels to the same extent as observed for a ts mutation of Pol II, suggesting that Mediator is essential for Pol II transcription in vivo (Thompson and Young, 1995; Holstege et al., 1998).

claim: mRNA measurements are complicated by effects on mRNA stability and hence do not directly assess Pol II transcription.
source: However, mRNA measurements are complicated by effects on mRNA stability and hence do not directly assess Pol II transcription.

source: Inactivation of Med17 causes decreased TBP occupancy at all promoters tested (Kuras and Struhl, 1999; Li et al., 1999), and genome-wide experiments show a general decrease in Pol II occupancy (Paul et al., 2015) and nascent transcription (Plaschka et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Genome-wide experiments show a general decrease in Pol II occupancy upon Med17 inactivation.
source: Inactivation of Med17 causes decreased TBP occupancy at all promoters tested (Kuras and Struhl, 1999; Li et al., 1999), and genome-wide experiments show a general decrease in Pol II occupancy (Paul et al., 2015) and nascent transcription (Plaschka et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Genome-wide experiments show a general decrease in nascent transcription upon Med17 inactivation.
source: Inactivation of Med17 causes decreased TBP occupancy at all promoters tested (Kuras and Struhl, 1999; Li et al., 1999), and genome-wide experiments show a general decrease in Pol II occupancy (Paul et al., 2015) and nascent transcription (Plaschka et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: There is substantial transcription in the absence of Med17 function.
source: However, our reanalysis of data from (Paul et al., 2015) reveals that this general decrease in Pol II occupancy is only 2–3 fold (see Results), suggesting that there is substantial transcription in the absence of Med17 function.
evidence: This is an inference based on the reanalysis of published data.

claim: In the med17-ts strain, transcription mediated by artificial recruitment of general transcription factors is reduced about 3-fold.
source: Consistent with this observation, in the med17-ts strain, transcription mediated by artificial recruitment of general transcription factors is reduced about 3-fold (Lacombe et al., 2013), and some genes can be activated (Lee and Lis, 1998; McNeil et al., 1998; Li et al., 1999).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: In the med17-ts strain, some genes can be activated.
source: Consistent with this observation, in the med17-ts strain, transcription mediated by artificial recruitment of general transcription factors is reduced about 3-fold (Lacombe et al., 2013), and some genes can be activated (Lee and Lis, 1998; McNeil et al., 1998; Li et al., 1999).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The med17-ts strains can grow at elevated temperatures in the presence of suppressor mutations in NC2.
source: In addition, the med17-ts strains can grow at elevated temperatures in the presence of suppressor mutations in NC2, a TBP-interacting complex (Gadbois et al., 1997).

claim: In the med17-ts strain, the head domain of Mediator breaks up.

claim: In the med17-ts strain, the tail module is still recruited to genes.

evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The tail module might contribute to the transcriptional function of Mediator in the med17-ts strain.
source: In the med17-ts strain, the head domain of Mediator breaks up, but the tail module is still recruited to genes (Linder et al., 2006; Paul et al., 2015) and might contribute to the transcriptional function of Mediator.

claim: Mediator modules that associate either with the enhancer or with the core promoter confer partial transcriptional activity.
source: Our results provide evidence that Mediator is essential for Pol II transcription in vivo, but that Mediator modules that associate either with the enhancer or with the core promoter confer partial transcriptional activity.

claim: Mediator inhibits promoter escape.

claim: Levels of the tagged Mediator subunits associated with the genome were reduced to background levels upon rapamycin addition.
source: Levels of the tagged Mediator subunits associated with the genome were reduced to background levels upon rapamycin addition (Petrenko et al., 2016); Figure 1A), indicating that the anchor-away procedure is efficient.

claim: The anchor-away procedure is efficient.
source: Levels of the tagged Mediator subunits associated with the genome were reduced to background levels upon rapamycin addition (Petrenko et al., 2016); Figure 1A), indicating that the anchor-away procedure is efficient.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that tagged subunits are reduced to background levels.

claim: Depletion of TBP or Pol II leads to a drastic decrease in transcription.

claim: For Mediator-depleted strains, the strongest decreases in Pol II occupancy are observed upon depletion of the essential head subunit Med17, the essential scaffold subunit Med14, and the essential middle subunit Med7.
source: For Mediator-depleted strains, the strongest decreases in Pol II occupancy are observed upon depletion of the essential head subunit Med17, the essential scaffold subunit Med14, and the essential middle subunit Med7.
evidence: This is an observation based on data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Depletion of Cdk8 has very modest effects on Pol II occupancy.
source: Depletion of Cdk8, the catalytic subunit of the kinase module, has very modest effects on Pol II occupancy (Figure 1B).

claim: Heat shock induction of HSP82 is reduced 2-fold in Med17-depleted cells.
source: In accord with modest transcriptional effects described above, heat shock induction of HSP82 and copper induction of CUP1 is reduced 2-fold in Med17-depleted cells (Figure 1C).

claim: Copper induction of CUP1 is reduced 2-fold in Med17-depleted cells.
source: In accord with modest transcriptional effects described above, heat shock induction of HSP82 and copper induction of CUP1 is reduced 2-fold in Med17-depleted cells (Figure 1C).

claim: Heat shock and copper induction in the med17-ts strain is consistent with previous observations.

claim: Reanalysis of published genome-scale Pol II occupancy data in a med17-ts strain reveals similar results to those obtained with the Med17-depletion strain.

claim: Loss of Med17 function leads to substantial transcription, albeit at an average 3-fold lower level.
source: Our reanalysis of published genome-scale Pol II occupancy data in a med17-ts strain (Paul et al., 2015) reveals similar results to those obtained here with the Med17-depletion strain (Figure 1—figure supplements 1A and 2); substantial transcription, albeit at an average 3-fold lower level upon loss of Med17 function.

claim: Loss of Med17 function leads to dissociation of other head and middle subunits from the enhancer, whereas the tail module remains.

claim: The stronger effect on SAGA-dependent genes observed under conditions of Med17 depletion also occurs in the med17-ts strain.

claim: Inactivation or depletion of Med17 by independent methods yields similar disruption of Mediator structure and quantitatively modest transcriptional effects.

claim: For all head, middle, and tail subunits tested, SAGA-dependent genes are more strongly affected by Mediator depletion than TFIID-dependent genes.

claim: The transcriptional profiles in Mediator-depletion strains are similar, though not identical.
source: The transcriptional profiles in these Mediator-depletion strains are similar, though not identical (Figure 2B).

claim: The relative importance of Mediator at SAGA-dependent vs. TFIID-dependent genes has been described in strains lacking the tail module.
source: The relative importance of Mediator at SAGA-dependent vs. TFIID-dependent genes has been described in strains lacking the tail module (Ansari et al., 2012; Paul et al., 2015), but our results confirm those on other Mediator subunits that were reported while this work was in progress (Jeronimo et al., 2016).

claim: The relative importance of Mediator for SAGA-dependent vs. TFIID-dependent genes is also observed for Kin28, the kinase subunit of TFIIH.
source: The relative importance of Mediator for SAGA-dependent vs. TFIID-dependent genes is also observed for Kin28, the kinase subunit of TFIIH (Wong et al., 2014).

claim: Depletion of Cdk8 kinase has only a minor effect on Pol II occupancy, with a distinct transcriptional profile that does not discriminate between SAGA- and TFIID-dependent genes.
source: In contrast, depletion of Cdk8 kinase has only a minor effect on Pol II occupancy, with a distinct transcriptional profile that does not discriminate between SAGA- and TFIID-dependent genes.

claim: Kin28-dependent phosphorylation of the Pol II CTD causes dissociation of Mediator from the PIC.
source: Kin28-dependent phosphorylation of the Pol II CTD causes dissociation of Mediator from the PIC (Jeronimo and Robert, 2014; Wong et al., 2014), which is important for efficient escape of Pol II from the promoter (Wong et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Depletion of Kin28 causes increased Mediator occupancy at the core promoter.

evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Depletion of Kin28 causes an upstream shift in the Pol II profile, indicative of a defect in promoter escape.
source: In particular, depletion of Kin28 causes increased Mediator occupancy at the core promoter (Jeronimo and Robert, 2014; Wong et al., 2014) and an upstream shift in the Pol II profile (Wong et al., 2014), indicative of a defect in promoter escape.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Depletion of Mediator head or middle subunits causes a downstream shift in the Pol II profile.

claim: The downstream shift in the Pol II profile is not observed upon depletion of Mediator subunits in the tail or kinase module.

claim: The Pol II profile is unaffected under conditions of TBP depletion, even though Pol II transcription is drastically reduced.

claim: The downstream shift in the Pol II profile upon Mediator depletion provides complementary evidence that Mediator, via the head and middle subunits, inhibits promoter escape in vivo.

claim: The Mediator:Pol II occupancy ratio at all genes tested upon simultaneous depletion of Med17 and Kin28 is far below the consistent ratio observed in Kin28 depletion strains.

claim: TBP and TFIIB occupancy at the core promoters is in excellent accord with Pol II occupancy in the coding regions, indicative of a functional PIC.

claim: Simultaneous depletion of Kin28 and TBP drastically reduces transcription and TBP, TFIIB, and Mediator occupancies at the core promoter.

claim: Under conditions where TBP/Kin28 depletion is less efficient, the level of transcription is reduced in accord with the reduction in TBP, TFIIB, and Mediator occupancy.

claim: In the absence of Kin28, depletion of TBP affects the level but not the composition of the PIC.
source: Thus, in the absence of Kin28, depletion of TBP affects the level but not the composition (i.e. the relative occupancy of the components) of the PIC, whereas depletion of Med17 alters the composition of a transcriptionally-competent PIC.
evidence: This is an inference based on data shown in Figure 5.

claim: In the absence of Kin28, depletion of Med17 alters the composition of a transcriptionally-competent PIC.
source: Thus, in the absence of Kin28, depletion of TBP affects the level but not the composition (i.e. the relative occupancy of the components) of the PIC, whereas depletion of Med17 alters the composition of a transcriptionally-competent PIC.
evidence: This is an inference based on data shown in Figure 4 and Figure 5.

claim: Pol II transcription and hence a functional PIC can occur in the absence of Mediator at the core promoter.
source: These observations suggest that Pol II transcription and hence a functional PIC can occur in the absence of Mediator at the core promoter, and hence that Mediator is not an essential component of the PIC in vivo (see Discussion).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on data shown in Figure 4 and Figure 5.

claim: Mediator can stimulate Kin28-dependent phosphorylation of the Pol II CTD at serine 5 residues in vitro.
source: Mediator can stimulate Kin28-dependent phosphorylation of the Pol II CTD at serine 5 residues in vitro (Guidi et al., 2004; Esnault et al., 2008; Nozawa et al., 2017), but this activity has never been examined in vivo.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Mediator's activity in stimulating Kin28-dependent phosphorylation of the Pol II CTD at serine 5 residues has never been examined in vivo.
source: Mediator can stimulate Kin28-dependent phosphorylation of the Pol II CTD at serine 5 residues in vitro (Guidi et al., 2004; Esnault et al., 2008; Nozawa et al., 2017), but this activity has never been examined in vivo.
evidence: This statement identifies a gap in knowledge that the study addresses.

claim: Depletion of all Mediator subunits tested causes decreased phosphorylation of serine 5 residues in the Pol II CTD at all core promoter regions examined.
source: In accord with the biochemical observations, depletion of all Mediator subunits tested causes decreased phosphorylation of serine 5 residues in the Pol II CTD (normalized to Pol II levels) at all core promoter regions examined (Figure 6).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 6.

claim: The level of CTD-serine 5 phosphorylation upon Mediator depletion is higher than observed when Kin28 is depleted.
source: However, the level of CTD-serine 5 phosphorylation upon Mediator depletion is higher than observed when Kin28 is depleted.
evidence: This is an observation based on data shown in Figure 6.

claim: CTD-serine 5 phosphorylation levels were low near the 3' end in all strains.
source: As expected (Komarnitsky et al., 2000), CTD-serine 5 phosphorylation levels were low near the 3' end in all strains (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1 and a citation to prior literature.

claim: Mediator contributes to, but is not fully responsible for, CTD-serine 5 phosphorylation in vivo.
source: Thus, Mediator contributes to, but is not fully responsible for, CTD-serine 5 phosphorylation in vivo.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on data shown in Figure 6.

claim: In the absence of rapamycin, Pol II levels at PMA1, CCW12, and TEF1 in the triple mutant strain are reduced compared to the wild-type.
source: In the absence of rapamycin, Pol II levels at PMA1, CCW12, and TEF1 in the triple mutant strain are reduced compared to the wild-type (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Depleting Med17 in the triple mutant strain causes a further decrease in transcription of PMA1, CCW12, and TEF1, close to or at the background level of detection.
source: Depleting Med17 in this strain causes a further decrease in transcription of all three genes, close to or at the background level of detection (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: The triple depletion strain can induce SSA4 and HSP82 upon heat shock or CUP1 in response to copper, albeit at a much lower level than wild-type cells or cells deleted either for the tail module or Med17.
source: The triple depletion strain can induce SSA4 and HSP82 upon heat shock or CUP1 in response to copper, albeit at a much lower level than wild-type cells or cells deleted either for the tail module (Figure 6A) or Med17 (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is an observation based on data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Comparably low levels of transcription are observed in a strain where Med3, Med15, and Med17 were simultaneously depleted via anchor-away.
source: Comparably low levels of transcription are observed in a strain where Med3, Med15, and Med17 were simultaneously depleted via anchor-away (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Simultaneous depletion of the essential subunits Med22 and Med7 results in substantial levels of transcription, comparable to that observed upon Med17 depletion.
source: In contrast, simultaneous depletion of the essential subunits Med22 (head module) and Med7 (middle module) results in substantial levels of transcription, comparable to that observed upon Med17 depletion (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Depletion of all three Mediator modules has a stronger transcriptional effect than conditions where the tail module is present at enhancers or the head and middle modules are present at core promoters.
source: Thus, depletion of all three Mediator modules has a stronger transcriptional effect than conditions where the tail module is present at enhancers (Med17 depletion) or the head and middle modules are present at core promoters (deletion of tail subunits).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on data shown in Figure 7.

claim: There is a very low level of transcriptional activation in TBP- or Pol II-depleted strains.
source: In both cases, there is a very low level of transcriptional activation, roughly comparable to (although perhaps slightly lower than) that occurring in the triple depletion strain.
evidence: This is an observation based on data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: The level of Pol II transcription upon depletion of all Mediator modules is indistinguishable from that occurring upon TBP depletion.
source: More generally, genome-scale, RNA-seq analysis indicates that the level of Pol II transcription upon depletion of all Mediator modules is indistinguishable from that occurring upon TBP depletion (Figure 7D).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: Most, and perhaps all, of the weak activation in the triple depletion strain reflects incomplete depletion of Mediator subunits.
source: These observations indicate that most, and perhaps all, of the weak activation in the triple depletion strain reflects incomplete depletion of Mediator subunits.
evidence: This is an inference based on comparison of data from triple depletion and TBP/Pol II depletion strains.

claim: For all 18 Mediator subunits tested, depletion of any individual subunit does not prevent cells from growing at 30°C.
source: For all 18 Mediator subunits tested, depletion of any individual subunit (or the combination of the essential subunits Med22 and Med7) does not prevent cells from growing at 30°C (Figure 8A).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 8A.

claim: Depletion of Mediator subunits by anchor-away is incomplete.
source: As deletion of some Mediator subunits prevents cell growth, these observations indicate that depletion of Mediator subunits by anchor-away is incomplete.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that cells can grow despite depletion of essential subunits.

claim: The Med17 and many other anchor-away strains are unable to grow at 37°C.
source: Interestingly, as seen in the med17-ts strain, the Med17 and many other anchor-away strains are unable to grow at 37°C (Figure 8B).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 8B.

claim: The failure of the med17-ts strain to grow at elevated temperature may not be due to complete inactivation of Med17 but rather the requirement for higher levels of Mediator function to support growth under stressful conditions.
source: As the med17-ts and Med17 depletion strains have effects on transcription (Figure 1C,D), the failure of the med17-ts strain to grow at elevated temperature may not be due to complete inactivation of Med17 but rather the requirement for higher levels of Mediator function to support growth under stressful conditions.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the observation that both strains show similar transcriptional effects but fail to grow at elevated temperature.

claim: Growth at 30°C is abolished upon depletion of individual subunits of any general transcription factor by the anchor-away method.
source: In striking contrast to all individual Mediator subunits tested, growth at 30°C is abolished upon depletion of individual subunits of any general transcription factor (TBP, TFIIA, TFIIB, TFIIE, TFIIF, TFIIH, Pol II) by the same anchor-away method (Figure 8A).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 8A.

claim: Simultaneous depletion/removal of all Mediator modules results in extremely poor growth at 30°C.
source: However, simultaneous depletion/removal of all Mediator modules (either by depleting Med17 in the tail deletion strain (med3∆ med15∆ med17-AA) or triple anchor-away depletion of the same subunits (med3-AA med15-AA med17-AA) results in extremely poor growth at 30°C (Figure 8C).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 8C.

claim: Depletion of all Mediator modules causes drastic effects on transcription and cell growth, whereas depletion of individual Mediator subunits has more modest effects.
source: Thus, depletion of all Mediator modules causes drastic effects on transcription and cell growth, whereas depletion of individual Mediator subunits has more modest effects.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on data shown in Figure 7 and Figure 8.

claim: Viability of Mediator-depletion strains is not due to incomplete depletion by the anchor-away method per se.
source: This striking dichotomy suggests that viability of Mediator-depletion strains is not due to incomplete depletion by the anchor-away method per se.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that triple depletion causes lethality while single depletions do not.

claim: Incomplete anchor-away-mediated depletion cannot easily explain why cells subject to simultaneous depletion of essential Mediator subunits in the head and middle module are viable, whereas cells simultaneously depleted of the essential Med17 and two non-essential tail subunits are inviable.
source: Moreover, incomplete anchor-away-mediated depletion cannot easily explain why cells subject to simultaneous depletion of essential Mediator subunits in the head (Med22) and middle (Med7) module are viable, whereas cells simultaneously depleted of the essential Med17 and two non-essential tail subunits (Med3 and Med15) are inviable.
evidence: This is an inference based on the differential effects of depleting different combinations of Mediator subunits.

claim: Transcription initiated from Mediator-lacking PICs is substantial but insufficient for cell growth.
source: To explain why some Mediator subunits are essential, we suggest that transcription initiated from Mediator-lacking PICs is substantial but insufficient for cell growth.
evidence: This is a speculation to explain the observation that cells can survive with reduced transcription from single Mediator depletions.

claim: Incomplete depletion of an essential subunit allows enough additional transcription to put cells over the life/death threshold.
source: Incomplete depletion of an essential subunit allows enough additional transcription to put cells over the life/death threshold.
evidence: This is a speculation to explain the viability of single Mediator depletion strains.

claim: The viable Mediator-depletion strains grow more slowly than parental strains at 30°C and not at all at 37°C.
source: Consistent with the idea of a viability threshold, the viable Mediator-depletion strains grow more slowly than parental strains at 30°C and not at all at 37°C.
evidence: This is an observation based on data shown in Figure 8.

claim: The difference between life and death could be due to overall reduced (but not eliminated) transcription or reduced transcription of one or more genes.
source: The difference between life and death could be due to overall reduced (but not eliminated) transcription or reduced transcription of one or more genes.
evidence: This is a speculation about the mechanism underlying the viability threshold.

claim: It is formally possible that Mediator might have some non-chromosomal function.
source: We also note that, unlike inducible degron-based methods (Dohmen et al., 1994; Moqtaderi et al., 1996; Nishimura et al., 2009), the anchor-away approach does not destroy the protein but rather anchors it to the ribosome. As such, it is formally possible that Mediator might have some non-chromosomal function, and in this regard Mediator has post-transcriptional roles (Carlsten et al., 2013; Conaway and Conaway, 2013; Allen and Taatjes, 2015).
evidence: This is a speculation about potential non-chromosomal functions of Mediator, supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Mediator has post-transcriptional roles.
source: We also note that, unlike inducible degron-based methods (Dohmen et al., 1994; Moqtaderi et al., 1996; Nishimura et al., 2009), the anchor-away approach does not destroy the protein but rather anchors it to the ribosome. As such, it is formally possible that Mediator might have some non-chromosomal function, and in this regard Mediator has post-transcriptional roles (Carlsten et al., 2013; Conaway and Conaway, 2013; Allen and Taatjes, 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Simultaneous depletion of subunits in the head, middle, and tail modules is the most stringent test of Mediator function in vivo.
source: Simultaneous depletion of subunits in the head, middle, and tail modules is the most stringent test of Mediator function in vivo.
evidence: This is a statement about the experimental approach used in the study.

claim: Under triple depletion conditions, there is a drastic effect on Pol II occupancy at genes expressed at steady-state prior to depletion or induced after depletion.
source: Under this condition (triple depletion strain), there is a drastic effect on Pol II occupancy at genes expressed at steady-state prior to depletion or induced after depletion.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 7.

claim: The magnitude of the transcriptional defect in the triple depletion strain is roughly comparable to that observed upon depletion of TBP or Pol II by the same method.
source: The magnitude of the transcriptional defect is roughly comparable to that observed upon depletion of TBP or Pol II by the same method.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 7.

claim: Cells depleted for all Mediator modules grow extremely poorly.
source: In addition, cells depleted for all Mediator modules grow extremely poorly, unlike the case for strains depleted for individual Mediator subunits.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 8C.

claim: The transcriptional and growth effects upon depletion of all Mediator modules may be slightly less pronounced than upon depletion of TBP or Pol II.
source: The transcriptional and growth effects upon depletion of all Mediator modules may be slightly less pronounced than upon depletion of TBP or Pol II.
evidence: This is an observation based on data shown in Figure 7 and Figure 8.

claim: Subtle differences between triple Mediator depletion and TBP/Pol II depletion could be due to a very low level of Mediator-independent transcription, or they might simply reflect a very subtle difference in depletion efficiency.
source: These subtle differences could be due to a very low level of Mediator-independent transcription, or they might simply reflect a very subtle difference in depletion efficiency, and hence be are an experimental artifact.
evidence: This is a speculation about the interpretation of the data.

claim: Depletion/inactivation of Med17 has a relatively modest transcriptional effect because the tail module remains associated with the enhancer.
source: In this view, depletion/inactivation of Med17 (and other essential subunits) has a relatively modest transcriptional effect, because the tail module remains associated with the enhancer.
evidence: This is a speculation about the mechanism underlying the modest transcriptional effect of Med17 depletion.

claim: The molecular basis of the tail-specific function is unknown.
source: The molecular basis of this tail-specific function is unknown, but it might reflect the ability of the tail module to interact with a component of the basic Pol II machinery and/or to increase the association of other co-activators (e.g. SAGA or Swi/Snf) with the enhancer.
evidence: This is a statement acknowledging a gap in knowledge.

claim: The tail module might interact with a component of the basic Pol II machinery.
source: The molecular basis of this tail-specific function is unknown, but it might reflect the ability of the tail module to interact with a component of the basic Pol II machinery and/or to increase the association of other co-activators (e.g. SAGA or Swi/Snf) with the enhancer.
evidence: This is a speculation about the potential function of the tail module.

claim: The tail module might increase the association of other co-activators with the enhancer.
source: The molecular basis of this tail-specific function is unknown, but it might reflect the ability of the tail module to interact with a component of the basic Pol II machinery and/or to increase the association of other co-activators (e.g. SAGA or Swi/Snf) with the enhancer.
evidence: This is a speculation about the potential function of the tail module.

claim: The tail module might increase recruitment of the very low levels of the head and middle subunits to the promoter, but not affect PIC function directly.
source: It is also possible that the tail module might increase recruitment of the very low levels of the head and middle subunits to the promoter, but not affect PIC function directly.
evidence: This is a speculation about the potential function of the tail module.

claim: Removal of the tail module has a relatively modest effect on Pol II transcription because the middle and head modules can associate with the PIC at the core promoter.
source: Conversely, removal of the tail module also has a relatively modest effect on Pol II transcription, because the middle and head modules can associate with the PIC at the core promoter (Jeronimo et al., 2016; Petrenko et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a speculation supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The independent functions of Mediator modules are consistent with the observation that SAGA-dependent genes are more affected than TFIID-dependent genes upon depletion of Mediator subunits.
source: The independent functions of Mediator modules are consistent with the observation that SAGA-dependent genes are more affected than TFIID-dependent genes upon depletion of Mediator subunits.
evidence: This is an inference connecting the independent functions of Mediator modules to the differential effects on gene classes.

claim: TFIID strengthens the interaction of the basic Pol II machinery with the core promoter via TAF-DNA interactions.
source: By virtue of TAF-DNA interactions (Verrijzer et al., 1995; Oelgeschläger et al., 1996; Burke and Kadonaga, 1997), TFIID strengthens the interaction of the basic Pol II machinery with the core promoter, thereby making the Mediator-dependent connection between enhancer and promoter less important at TFIID-dependent genes.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: TFIID makes the Mediator-dependent connection between enhancer and promoter less important at TFIID-dependent genes.
source: By virtue of TAF-DNA interactions (Verrijzer et al., 1995; Oelgeschläger et al., 1996; Burke and Kadonaga, 1997), TFIID strengthens the interaction of the basic Pol II machinery with the core promoter, thereby making the Mediator-dependent connection between enhancer and promoter less important at TFIID-dependent genes.
evidence: This is an inference based on the role of TFIID in strengthening PIC-promoter interactions.

claim: Transcription of SAGA-dependent genes relies on TBP, not TFIID.
source: In contrast, transcription of SAGA-dependent genes relies on TBP, not TFIID, and hence Mediator is needed to efficiently connect the enhancer and core promoter.
evidence: This statement is based on established knowledge about SAGA-dependent genes.

claim: Mediator is needed to efficiently connect the enhancer and core promoter at SAGA-dependent genes.
source: In contrast, transcription of SAGA-dependent genes relies on TBP, not TFIID, and hence Mediator is needed to efficiently connect the enhancer and core promoter.
evidence: This is an inference based on the differential requirements of SAGA-dependent genes.

claim: Mediator is not required for basal transcription and hence PIC formation in vitro.
source: Furthermore, unlike general transcription factors, Mediator is not required for basal transcription and hence PIC formation in vitro.
evidence: This statement is based on established knowledge from in vitro transcription studies.

claim: Cells depleted simultaneously for Med17 and Kin28 support substantial Pol II transcription even though a very low level of Mediator is detected at the core promoter.
source: First, and most directly, cells depleted simultaneously for Med17 and Kin28 support substantial Pol II transcription even though a very low level of Mediator is detected at the core promoter.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4.

claim: TBP and TFIIB occupancies in cells depleted simultaneously for Med17 and Kin28 are in accord with Pol II occupancy, indicative of a functional PIC in the apparent absence of Mediator.
source: Furthermore, TBP and TFIIB occupancies in such cells are in accord with Pol II occupancy, indicative of a functional PIC in the apparent absence of Mediator.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Cells depleted only for Kin28 have a much higher level of Mediator at the core promoter, even though Pol II, TBP, and TFIIB occupancies are comparable to cells depleted for both Med17 and Kin28.
source: In contrast, cells depleted only for Kin28 have a much higher level of Mediator at the core promoter, even though Pol II, TBP, and TFIIB occupancies are comparable.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Low Mediator:Pol II, Mediator:TBP, and Mediator:TFIIB occupancy ratios at the core promoter upon simultaneous depletion of Med17 and Kin28 provides very strong evidence of a transcriptionally competent, Mediator-independent PIC.
source: These low Mediator:Pol II, Mediator:TBP, and Mediator:TFIIB occupancy ratios at the core promoter upon simultaneous depletion of Med17 and Kin28 provides very strong evidence of a transcriptionally competent, Mediator-independent PIC.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on data shown in Figure 4.

claim: The conclusion that Mediator is not an obligate component of the PIC does not rely on the degree of Mediator depletion per se, but rather direct observation at the core promoter.
source: As discussed below, this conclusion does not rely on the degree of Mediator depletion per se, but rather direct observation at the core promoter.
evidence: This is a statement about the interpretation of the data.

claim: The non-wild-type Pol II profile upon Mediator depletion is very difficult to explain by incomplete depletion per se.
source: Second, depletion of Mediator head or middle subunits causes a downstream shift in the Pol II occupancy profile. This non-wild-type Pol II profile is very difficult to explain by incomplete depletion per se (see below), and hence it strongly supports the idea of transcription initiated from a PIC lacking Mediator.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation of the downstream shift in Pol II occupancy.

claim: The downstream shift in the Pol II profile strongly supports the idea of transcription initiated from a PIC lacking Mediator.
source: Second, depletion of Mediator head or middle subunits causes a downstream shift in the Pol II occupancy profile. This non-wild-type Pol II profile is very difficult to explain by incomplete depletion per se (see below), and hence it strongly supports the idea of transcription initiated from a PIC lacking Mediator.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation of the downstream shift in Pol II occupancy.

claim: The downstream shift in the Pol II profile is not observed upon depletion of tail subunits that do not directly interact with general transcription factors at the PIC, yet have comparable quantitative effects on Pol II occupancy.
source: Notably, this downstream shift in the Pol II profile is not observed upon depletion of tail subunits that do not directly interact with general transcription factors at the PIC, yet have comparable quantitative effects on Pol II occupancy.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The dichotomy between Mediator and general transcription factors with respect to growth properties upon depletion supports the conclusion that Mediator is not an obligate component of the PIC.
source: In addition to these two major arguments, our conclusion is supported by the dichotomy between Mediator and general transcription factors with respect to growth properties upon depletion.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that cells can grow when Mediator is depleted but not when general transcription factors are depleted.

claim: Mediator is not completely depleted in the experiments.
source: Mediator is not completely depleted in our experiments, and complete elimination of any essential protein is impossible.
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of the limitations of the experimental approach.

claim: Complete elimination of any essential protein is impossible.
source: Mediator is not completely depleted in our experiments, and complete elimination of any essential protein is impossible.
evidence: This is a statement about the inherent limitations of studying essential proteins.

claim: The definition of incomplete depletion is that the small amount of remaining protein is structurally and functionally identical to the protein prior to depletion.
source: However, the definition of incomplete depletion is that the small amount of remaining protein is structurally and functionally identical to the protein prior to depletion.
evidence: This is a definition provided by the authors.

claim: Incomplete depletion of a general transcription factor will reduce (but not eliminate) transcription and its occupancy at the core promoter, but it will not affect either the relative ratios of general transcription factors at core promoters or the Pol II profile.
source: Thus, incomplete depletion of a general transcription factor will reduce (but not eliminate) transcription and its occupancy at the core promoter, but it will not affect either the relative ratios of general transcription factors at core promoters (i.e. PIC level) or the Pol II profile.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the expected effects of incomplete depletion.

claim: Incomplete depletion of TBP reduces transcription and also reduces to comparable extents the levels of general transcription factors and Mediator at the core promoter.
source: Indeed, incomplete depletion of TBP not only reduces transcription, but it also reduces to comparable extents the levels of general transcription factors and Mediator at the core promoter.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Depletion of Med17 drastically reduces Mediator occupancy at the core promoter, whereas it has only modest and comparable effects on occupancy of TBP, TFIIB, and Pol II.
source: In contrast, depletion of Med17 drastically reduces Mediator occupancy at the core promoter, whereas it has only modest and comparable effects on occupancy of TBP, TFIIB, and Pol II.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Incomplete depletion of Mediator cannot explain the key observations that Mediator is not an obligate component of the PIC.
source: Thus, as incomplete depletion of Mediator cannot explain the key observations, our results indicate that (1) Mediator is not an obligate component of the PIC, (2) transcription can occur from a PIC lacking Mediator, and (3) that transcription from a Mediator-lacking PIC escapes the promoter more easily than a Mediator-containing PIC.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the data and logical reasoning.

claim: Transcription can occur from a PIC lacking Mediator.
source: Thus, as incomplete depletion of Mediator cannot explain the key observations, our results indicate that (1) Mediator is not an obligate component of the PIC, (2) transcription can occur from a PIC lacking Mediator, and (3) that transcription from a Mediator-lacking PIC escapes the promoter more easily than a Mediator-containing PIC.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the data and logical reasoning.

claim: Transcription from a Mediator-lacking PIC escapes the promoter more easily than a Mediator-containing PIC.
source: Thus, as incomplete depletion of Mediator cannot explain the key observations, our results indicate that (1) Mediator is not an obligate component of the PIC, (2) transcription can occur from a PIC lacking Mediator, and (3) that transcription from a Mediator-lacking PIC escapes the promoter more easily than a Mediator-containing PIC.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the downstream shift in Pol II occupancy upon Mediator depletion.

claim: One possibility is that Mediator performs a catalytic function at the core promoter that alters the activity of the PIC in a manner that is essential for transcription.
source: One possibility is that Mediator performs a catalytic function at the core promoter that alters the activity of the PIC in a manner that is essential for transcription.
evidence: This is a speculation about the mechanism by which Mediator is essential for transcription.

claim: Mediator can affect the conformation of Pol II.
source: However, Mediator can affect the conformation of Pol II (Plaschka et al., 2015; Tsai et al., 2017), so a Mediator-induced conformational effect could be a catalytic, yet essential function for Pol II transcription.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: A Mediator-induced conformational effect could be a catalytic, yet essential function for Pol II transcription.
source: However, Mediator can affect the conformation of Pol II (Plaschka et al., 2015; Tsai et al., 2017), so a Mediator-induced conformational effect could be a catalytic, yet essential function for Pol II transcription.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the observation that Mediator can affect Pol II conformation.

claim: Biochemical experiments have suggested that Mediator functions as an assembly factor that facilitates PIC maturation through different stages.
source: In addition, biochemical experiments have suggested that Mediator functions as an assembly factor that facilitates PIC maturation through different stages (Malik et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: The tail module that remains associated at the enhancer upon Med17 depletion could have an independent transcriptional function that does not involve its connection to the middle and head modules.
source: Alternatively, the tail module that remains associated at the enhancer upon Med17 depletion could have an independent transcriptional function that does not involve its connection to the middle and head modules.
evidence: This is a speculation about the mechanism by which Mediator is essential for transcription.

claim: The tail module could interact directly with Pol II or a general transcription factor, thereby stimulating PIC formation.
source: For example, the tail module could interact directly with Pol II or a general transcription factor, thereby stimulating PIC formation.
evidence: This is a speculation about the potential function of the tail module.

claim: The tail module might indirectly stimulate PIC formation via a direct interaction with the SAGA co-activator complex.
source: The tail module might indirectly stimulate PIC formation via a direct interaction with the SAGA co-activator complex, whose Spt3 subunit of SAGA interacts with TBP.
evidence: This is a speculation about the potential function of the tail module.

claim: The Spt3 subunit of SAGA interacts with TBP.
source: The tail module might indirectly stimulate PIC formation via a direct interaction with the SAGA co-activator complex, whose Spt3 subunit of SAGA interacts with TBP.
evidence: This statement is based on established knowledge.

claim: The proposed mechanism would permit increased recruitment of a Mediator-lacking PIC.
source: This suggested mechanism would not only permit increased recruitment of a Mediator-lacking PIC, but it would also explain the observation that SAGA-dependent genes are more affected than TFIID-dependent genes upon depletion of Mediator subunits.
evidence: This is a speculation about the implications of the proposed mechanism.

claim: The proposed mechanism would explain the observation that SAGA-dependent genes are more affected than TFIID-dependent genes upon depletion of Mediator subunits.
source: This suggested mechanism would not only permit increased recruitment of a Mediator-lacking PIC, but it would also explain the observation that SAGA-dependent genes are more affected than TFIID-dependent genes upon depletion of Mediator subunits.
evidence: This is a speculation about the implications of the proposed mechanism.

claim: The anchor-away method permits the rapid removal of proteins from the nucleus under conditions where cells are not stressed by heat shock or other environmental insults.
source: The anchor-away method permits the rapid removal of proteins from the nucleus under conditions where cells are not stressed by heat shock or other environmental insults (Haruki et al., 2008).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Cells are treated with rapamycin to induce the anchor-away process.
source: Although cells are treated with rapamycin to induce the anchor-away process, the strains carry the tor1-1 mutation that blocks the physiological effects of rapamycin.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental method.

claim: The strains carry the tor1-1 mutation that blocks the physiological effects of rapamycin.
source: Although cells are treated with rapamycin to induce the anchor-away process, the strains carry the tor1-1 mutation that blocks the physiological effects of rapamycin.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental method.

claim: Control anchor-away strains show comparable Pol II occupancy profiles in the presence or absence of rapamycin.
source: Most importantly, control anchor-away strains show comparable Pol II occupancy profiles in the presence or absence of rapamycin (Wong et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior literature.
